claim: Somatic cell nuclear transfer has established that the oocyte contains maternal factors with epigenetic reprogramming capacity.
source: Somatic cell nuclear transfer has established that the oocyte contains maternal factors with epigenetic reprogramming capacity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about SCNT and oocyte reprogramming capacity.

claim: In C. elegans, LSD1/KDM1A enables the gamete to embryo transition by removing H3K4me2 and preventing the transgenerational inheritance of transcription patterns.
source: In C. elegans, LSD1/KDM1A enables this transition by removing H3K4me2 and preventing the transgenerational inheritance of transcription patterns.
evidence: This statement references prior work on C. elegans LSD1/KDM1A function, which is cited elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of maternal LSD1/KDM1A in mice results in embryonic arrest at the 1-2 cell stage.
source: Here we show that loss of maternal LSD1/KDM1A in mice results in embryonic arrest at the 1-2 cell stage, with arrested embryos failing to undergo the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Embryos arrested at the 1-2 cell stage fail to undergo the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
source: Here we show that loss of maternal LSD1/KDM1A in mice results in embryonic arrest at the 1-2 cell stage, with arrested embryos failing to undergo the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing failure of zygotic genome activation.

claim: LSD1/KDM1A maternal reprogramming is conserved between C. elegans and mice.
source: This suggests that LSD1/KDM1A maternal reprogramming is conserved.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar phenotypes observed in both organisms.

claim: Partial loss of maternal LSD1/KDM1A results in perinatal lethality.
source: Moreover, partial loss of maternal LSD1/KDM1A results in striking phenotypes weeks after fertilization; including perinatal lethality and abnormal behavior in surviving adults.
evidence: This is supported by data from Kdm1aVasa mutants showing increased perinatal death.

claim: Partial loss of maternal LSD1/KDM1A results in abnormal behavior in surviving adults.
source: Moreover, partial loss of maternal LSD1/KDM1A results in striking phenotypes weeks after fertilization; including perinatal lethality and abnormal behavior in surviving adults.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral assays including marble burying and open field tests.

claim: Maternal effect hypomorphic phenotypes are associated with alterations in DNA methylation at imprinted genes.
source: These maternal effect hypomorphic phenotypes are associated with alterations in DNA methylation and expression at imprinted genes.
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data showing altered methylation at imprinted loci.

claim: Maternal effect hypomorphic phenotypes are associated with alterations in expression at imprinted genes.
source: These maternal effect hypomorphic phenotypes are associated with alterations in DNA methylation and expression at imprinted genes.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing altered expression of imprinted genes.

claim: Defects in early epigenetic reprogramming can lead to defects that manifest later in development.
source: These results establish a novel mammalian paradigm where defects in early epigenetic reprogramming can lead to defects that manifest later in development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that early loss of maternal KDM1A leads to perinatal and adult phenotypes.

claim: At fertilization, the epigenome of the developing zygote undergoes widespread changes in DNA methylation and histone methylation.
source: At fertilization, the epigenome of the developing zygote undergoes widespread changes in DNA methylation and histone methylation (Aoki et al., 1997; Arico et al., 2011; Bultman et al., 2006; Burton and Torres-Padilla, 2010; Lindeman et al., 2011; Smith et al., 2012; Vastenhouw et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Epigenetic reprogramming at fertilization is driven by the deposition of maternal proteins and RNA into the zygote.
source: This reprogramming is driven by the deposition of maternal proteins and RNA into the zygote (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: After fertilization, zygotic genes become transcriptionally active while the maternal transcriptional program is silenced.
source: After fertilization, zygotic genes become transcriptionally active, while the maternal transcriptional program is silenced (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In mice, the maternal-to-zygotic transition occurs between the one- and two-cell stage.
source: In mice, this maternal-to-zygotic transition (MZT) occurs between the one- and two-cell (1-2C) stage (Aoki et al., 1997; Hamatani et al., 2004; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Somatic cell nuclear transfer experiments in Xenopus demonstrated that the oocyte has the capacity to reprogram a differentiated somatic nucleus into a cloned embryo.
source: Somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT) experiments in Xenopus demonstrated that the oocyte has the capacity to reprogram a differentiated somatic nucleus into a cloned embryo (Gurdon et al., 1958).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the classic Gurdon work.

claim: The epigenetic reprogramming capacity of the oocyte is conserved in mammals.
source: This epigenetic reprogramming capacity of the oocyte is also conserved in mammals (Campbell et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on mammalian cloning.

claim: The epigenetic reprogramming capacity of the oocyte enables the maternal-to-zygotic transition.
source: It is thought that the epigenetic reprogramming capacity of the oocyte enables the MZT.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge.

claim: The enzymes involved in maternal epigenetic reprogramming largely remain a mystery.
source: Nevertheless, the enzymes involved in maternal epigenetic reprogramming, and the consequences of failure to reprogram, largely remain a mystery.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: H3K4me2 is acquired in gamete genes during the specification and maintenance of the germline in C. elegans.
source: Di-methylation of lysine 4 on histone H3 (H3K4me2) is acquired in gamete genes during the specification and maintenance of the germline.
evidence: This is based on prior work in C. elegans cited elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: The H3K4me2 demethylase KDM1A is maternally deposited into the zygote at fertilization in C. elegans.
source: The H3K4me2 demethylase KDM1A is maternally deposited into the zygote at fertilization and required to prevent H3K4me2 from being inherited transgenerationally.
evidence: This is based on prior work in C. elegans.

claim: KDM1A is required to prevent H3K4me2 from being inherited transgenerationally in C. elegans.
source: The H3K4me2 demethylase KDM1A is maternally deposited into the zygote at fertilization and required to prevent H3K4me2 from being inherited transgenerationally.
evidence: This is based on prior work in C. elegans.

claim: Without KDM1A, H3K4me2 accumulates at gamete genes across generations in C. elegans.
source: Without KDM1A, H3K4me2 accumulates at gamete genes across generations and results in the inappropriate expression of these genes.
evidence: This is based on prior work in C. elegans.

claim: Loss of KDM1A in C. elegans results in inappropriate expression of gamete genes.
source: Without KDM1A, H3K4me2 accumulates at gamete genes across generations and results in the inappropriate expression of these genes.
evidence: This is based on prior work in C. elegans.

claim: Loss of KDM1A in C. elegans correlates with increasing sterility in the population over time.
source: This correlates with increasing sterility in the population over time (Katz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on prior work cited.

claim: Reprogramming H3K4 methylation is a critical step in somatic cell nuclear transfer.
source: The requirement to reprogram H3K4 methylation is also suggested to be a critical step in SCNT.
evidence: This is inferred from SCNT experiments described in the following sentences.

claim: During SCNT in Xenopus, cloned embryos often inappropriately express genes from the tissue where the somatic nucleus was derived.
source: During SCNT in Xenopus, the cloned embryos often inappropriately express genes from the tissue where the somatic nucleus was derived (Ng and Gurdon, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Transcriptional memory in SCNT embryos can be eliminated by overexpressing histone H3 with a mutated K4 residue.
source: This transcriptional memory can be eliminated by overexpressing histone H3 with a mutated K4 residue (Ng and Gurdon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: H3K4 methylation may be the carrier of transgenerational transcriptional memory.
source: This work implies that H3K4 methylation may be the carrier of transgenerational transcriptional memory, and that complete reprogramming may require the removal of this modification.
evidence: This is inferred from the SCNT experiments with mutated H3.

claim: Complete epigenetic reprogramming may require the removal of H3K4 methylation.
source: This work implies that H3K4 methylation may be the carrier of transgenerational transcriptional memory, and that complete reprogramming may require the removal of this modification.
evidence: This is inferred from the SCNT experiments.

claim: Genomic imprinting is the monoallelic expression of a small number of genes based on their parent of origin.
source: Genomic imprinting is the monoallelic expression of a small number of genes based on their parent of origin (Bartolomei and Tilghman, 1997).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation.

claim: Imprinted genes are dependent upon DNA methylation at small imprinting control regions.
source: Imprinted genes are dependent upon DNA methylation at small imprinting control regions (ICRs) associated with these loci (Bartolomei and Tilghman, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: At ICRs, CpG methylation is established in the gametes and maintained throughout the development of the offspring.
source: At ICRs, CpG methylation is established in the gametes and maintained throughout the development of the offspring (Bartolomei, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: In mammals, there are two amine-oxidase histone demethylases, LSD2/KDM1B and KDM1A.
source: In mammals, there are two amine-oxidase histone demethylases, LSD2/KDM1B (hereafter referred to as KDM1B) and KDM1A (Ciccone et al., 2009; Shi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KDM1B is expressed mainly in the oocyte.
source: KDM1B is expressed mainly in the oocyte and required for the establishment of maternal imprints at imprinted loci (Ciccone et al., 2009; Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KDM1B is required for the establishment of maternal imprints at imprinted loci.
source: KDM1B is expressed mainly in the oocyte and required for the establishment of maternal imprints at imprinted loci (Ciccone et al., 2009; Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Without KDM1B, embryos derived from oocytes exhibit a maternal effect embryonic lethality phenotype prior to mid-gestation.
source: Without KDM1B, embryos derived from these oocytes exhibit a maternal effect embryonic lethality phenotype prior to mid-gestation (Ciccone et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Amine oxidase-type histone demethylases can function maternally in mammals.
source: This demonstrates that, similar to C. elegans, amine oxidase-type histone demethylases can function maternally in mammals.
evidence: This is inferred from the KDM1B maternal function.

claim: KDM1A is a component of several protein complexes.
source: KDM1A is a component of several protein complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about KDM1A.

claim: As part of the CoREST complex, KDM1A specifically demethylates H3K4me1/2, but not H3K4me3.
source: As part of the CoREST complex, it specifically demethylates H3K4me1/2, but not H3K4me3 (Shi et al., 2004; You et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When associated with the Androgen Receptor complex, KDM1A has been shown to demethylate H3K9me2 in vitro.
source: Alternatively, when associated with the Androgen Receptor complex KDM1A has been shown to demethylate H3K9me2 in vitro (Metzger et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: KDM1A is an essential gene in mammalian development.
source: KDM1A is an essential gene in mammalian development, as homozygous mutants fail to develop properly after implantation and die prior to embryonic day 8 (e8) (Foster et al., 2010; Macfarlan et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Homozygous KDM1A mutants fail to develop properly after implantation and die prior to embryonic day 8.
source: KDM1A is an essential gene in mammalian development, as homozygous mutants fail to develop properly after implantation and die prior to embryonic day 8 (e8) (Foster et al., 2010; Macfarlan et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: KDM1A is expressed throughout oocyte development.
source: KDM1A is expressed throughout oocyte development
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: RNA-seq datasets from ovulated oocytes and 2C-stage embryos show abundant KDM1A transcripts.
source: RNA-seq datasets from ovulated oocytes and 2C-stage embryos suggested abundant KDM1A transcripts in these cells (Macfarlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior RNA-seq data.

claim: Immunofluorescence and immunohistochemistry confirm that KDM1A is expressed in the oocyte nucleus and in the surrounding follicle cells throughout oocyte development.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) and immunohistochemistry (IHC) with an antibody raised against KDM1A confirms that KDM1A is expressed in the oocyte nucleus and in the surrounding follicle cells throughout oocyte development (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–L).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in figures.

claim: Deletion of Kdm1a with Gdf9-Cre results in the complete loss of KDM1A from the oocyte nucleus.
source: KDM1A IHC and IF demonstrate that deletion of Kdm1a with either Gdf9-Cre or Zp3-Cre results in the complete loss of KDM1A from the oocyte nucleus (Figure 1C–F,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of Kdm1a with Zp3-Cre results in the complete loss of KDM1A from the oocyte nucleus.
source: KDM1A IHC and IF demonstrate that deletion of Kdm1a with either Gdf9-Cre or Zp3-Cre results in the complete loss of KDM1A from the oocyte nucleus (Figure 1C–F,I).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Crossing the Kdm1afl/fl allele to Vasa-Cre results in complete maternal deletion, as determined by 100% segregation of the maternally deleted allele to offspring.
source: Crossing the Kdm1afl/fl allele to Vasa-Cre also results in complete maternal deletion, as can be determined by the 100% segregation of the maternally deleted allele to the offspring (all of offspring from Kdm1aVasa mothers crossed to wild-type fathers result in heterozygous -/+ offspring) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by genetic segregation data.

claim: Deletion of Kdm1a with Vasa-Cre results in a hypomorphic effect, where 33.3% of oocytes completely lack KDM1A protein, but 66.7% retain a low level of KDM1A.
source: However, for reasons that are not clear, deletion of Kdm1a with Vasa-Cre results in a hypomorphic effect, where 33.3% of oocytes completely lack KDM1A protein, but 66.7% retain a low level of KDM1A (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Vasa-Cre transgene is reported to be expressed earlier in the germline than either Gdf9-Cre or Zp3-Cre.
source: This incomplete effect is surprising because the Vasa-Cre transgene is reported to be expressed earlier in the germline than either Gdf9-Cre or Zp3-Cre (Figure 1B) (Gallardo et al., 2007; Lan et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on Cre expression timing.

claim: The low level of KDM1A remaining in some oocytes may be due to delayed deletion of Kdm1a.
source: It is possible that the low level of KDM1A remaining in some oocytes is due to delayed deletion of Kdm1a, though the reason for this potential delay is unknown.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of incomplete deletion.

claim: Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos exhibit embryonic arrest at the 1-2C stage.
source: Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos exhibit embryonic arrest at the 1-2C stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–I).
evidence: This is supported by embryo staging data shown in figures.

claim: In control Kdm1aGdf9 M+Z+ embryos at e1.5, 7% are fragmented/degraded, 65% are 1-cell embryos, and 28% are 2-cell embryos.
source: Specifically, in control Kdm1aGdf9 M+Z+ embryos at embryonic day 1.5 (e1.5), we observe 7% fragmented/degraded embryos, 65% 1-cell embryos and 28% 2-cell embryos (n=135, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryo staging data.

claim: In Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos at e1.5, 40% are fragmented/degraded, 59% are unfertilized oocytes or 1-cell embryos, and only 1% are 2C embryos.
source: In contrast, in Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos at e1.5 we observe 40% fragmented/degraded embryos, 59% unfertilized oocytes or 1-cell embryos, and only 1% 2C embryos (n=134, Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryo staging data.

claim: The vast majority of non-degraded Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos are clearly fertilized and arrested at the 1C stage.
source: The vast majority of the non-degraded Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos are clearly fertilized and arrested at the 1C stage.
evidence: This is based on observation of embryo morphology.

claim: Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos have a large increase in the number of fragmented/degraded embryos at the expense of normal 2C embryos compared to controls.
source: Nevertheless, compared to Kdm1aGdf9 M+Z+ embryos, Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos have a large increase in the number of fragmented/degraded embryos at the expense of normal 2C embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryo staging data.

claim: The remaining 1C and 2C Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos do not progress beyond the 1-2C stage.
source: Also, the remaining 1C and 2C Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos do not progress beyond the 1-2C stage, as we never observe any later stage embryos even at e2.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,G,H).
evidence: This is supported by embryo staging data at e2.5.

claim: At e1.5, 95% of control Kdm1aZp3 M+Z+ embryos have reached the 2C stage.
source: At e1.5, 95% (n=20) of control Kdm1aZp3 M+Z+ embryos have reached the 2C stage (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryo staging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At e1.5, only 35% of Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos reach the 2C stage.
source: In contrast, at e1.5 only 35% (n=57) of Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos reach the 2C stage (Figure 2E), though this is still much higher than the 1% of Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos that reach the 2C stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryo staging data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Two Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos develop past the 2C stage to the 3C- and 4C- stage.
source: In addition, we have observed two Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos that develop past the 2C stage to the 3C- and 4C- stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J,K), though like the Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos, no Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos survive to the blastocyst stage (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by observation of embryos shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J,K.

claim: No Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos survive to the blastocyst stage.
source: In addition, we have observed two Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos that develop past the 2C stage to the 3C- and 4C- stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J,K), though like the Kdm1aGdf9 M-Z+ embryos, no Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos survive to the blastocyst stage (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on observation of embryos.

claim: The embryonic arrest primarily at the 1-2C stages is the KDM1A maternal loss-of-function phenotype.
source: Taken together, the results from Kdm1aGdf9 and Kdm1aZp3 mice suggest that the embryonic arrest, primarily at the 1-2C stages is the KDM1A maternal loss-of-function phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data from both Cre lines.

claim: There are relatively few transcriptional changes in Kdm1aZp3 mutant oocytes compared to control oocytes.
source: We found relatively few transcriptional changes, with 195 genes over expressed and 281 genes under expressed in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 195 genes are over expressed in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes compared to control.
source: We found relatively few transcriptional changes, with 195 genes over expressed and 281 genes under expressed in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 281 genes are under expressed in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes compared to control.
source: We found relatively few transcriptional changes, with 195 genes over expressed and 281 genes under expressed in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Only 2 repeat families are activated and 2 repressed in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes.
source: In addition, amongst the 875 repeat types extracted from the RepeatMasker database (including LINEs, SINEs, etc.) there were only 2 repeat families that were activated and 2 repressed in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1A, Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The Mt1 gene is very highly activated in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes.
source: Manual inspection revealed that few of these genes/repeats had both large fold-changes and low p-values, with the exception of the Mt1 gene, which was very highly activated in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes.
evidence: This is based on manual inspection of RNA-seq data.

claim: Several mitochondrially encoded genes have small but significantly reduced levels in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes.
source: Furthermore, we found several mitochondrially encoded genes (like mtCo3 and Atpase6) that had small but significantly reduced levels in Kdm1aZp3 oocytes.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claim: Mitochondrial genes are unlikely to be directly regulated by KDM1A.
source: These mitochondrial genes are unlikely to be directly regulated by KDM1A, but their reduced levels could indicate a subtle metabolic defect in the mutants.
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of mitochondrial gene regulation.

claim: Reduced levels of mitochondrial genes could indicate a subtle metabolic defect in Kdm1aZp3 mutant oocytes.
source: These mitochondrial genes are unlikely to be directly regulated by KDM1A, but their reduced levels could indicate a subtle metabolic defect in the mutants.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data.

claim: Loss of KDM1A has little effect on transcription in oocytes.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that loss of KDM1A has little effect on transcription in oocytes.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing few transcriptional changes.

claim: There is a dramatic alteration of the transcriptome in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos compared to control 2C embryos.
source: We found a dramatic alteration of the transcriptome, with 1527 genes over expressed and 2794 genes under expressed in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 1527 genes are over expressed in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos compared to control.
source: We found a dramatic alteration of the transcriptome, with 1527 genes over expressed and 2794 genes under expressed in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 2794 genes are under expressed in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos compared to control.
source: We found a dramatic alteration of the transcriptome, with 1527 genes over expressed and 2794 genes under expressed in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: 103 repeat families are repressed in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos.
source: In addition, there were 103 repeat families that were repressed in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos, compared with only 5 that were activated (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Only 5 repeat families are activated in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos.
source: In addition, there were 103 repeat families that were repressed in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos, compared with only 5 that were activated (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The transcriptional changes in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos are in contrast to what has been observed in Kdm1a mutant ES cells.
source: These findings are in contrast to what has been observed in Kdm1a mutant ES cells that display a general de-repression of both genes and repeats (Macfarlan et al., 2011; Macfarlan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work on ES cells.

claim: GO analysis of genes in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos shows enrichment of genes normally expressed in unfertilized oocytes.
source: GO analysis of over and under expressed genes in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos demonstrated an enrichment of genes normally expressed in unfertilized oocytes, and a reduction in genes associated with embryonic development and tissue specific gene expression.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: GO analysis of genes in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos shows a reduction in genes associated with embryonic development and tissue specific gene expression.
source: GO analysis of over and under expressed genes in Kdm1aZp3 2C M-Z+ embryos demonstrated an enrichment of genes normally expressed in unfertilized oocytes, and a reduction in genes associated with embryonic development and tissue specific gene expression.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos may fail to undergo the MZT.
source: This suggests that Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos may fail to undergo the MZT (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the GO analysis results.

claim: In Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos relative to oocytes, there are massive changes in the mRNA profile with >3,000 genes becoming zygotically activated.
source: In Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos relative to Kdm1afl/fl oocytes, there are massive changes in the mRNA profile, with >3,000 genes (and 387 repeat families) becoming zygotically activated and ~3000 maternal genes (and 17 repeat families) which are suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data comparing oocytes and 2C embryos.

claim: In Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos relative to oocytes, 387 repeat families become zygotically activated.
source: In Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos relative to Kdm1afl/fl oocytes, there are massive changes in the mRNA profile, with >3,000 genes (and 387 repeat families) becoming zygotically activated and ~3000 maternal genes (and 17 repeat families) which are suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: In Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos relative to oocytes, ~3000 maternal genes are suppressed.
source: In Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos relative to Kdm1afl/fl oocytes, there are massive changes in the mRNA profile, with >3,000 genes (and 387 repeat families) becoming zygotically activated and ~3000 maternal genes (and 17 repeat families) which are suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: In Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos relative to oocytes, 17 repeat families are suppressed.
source: In Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos relative to Kdm1afl/fl oocytes, there are massive changes in the mRNA profile, with >3,000 genes (and 387 repeat families) becoming zygotically activated and ~3000 maternal genes (and 17 repeat families) which are suppressed.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The massive changes in mRNA profile in control 2C embryos demonstrate that MZT has occurred.
source: This demonstrates that MZT has occurred (Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1C).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data.

claim: Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos fail to properly activate the zygotic genome, with only 666 genes becoming activated.
source: In contrast, Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos fail to properly activate the zygotic genome, with only 666 genes becoming activated (and 110 repeat families), and only ~1200 maternal genes repressed (13 repeat families) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos, 110 repeat families become activated.
source: In contrast, Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos fail to properly activate the zygotic genome, with only 666 genes becoming activated (and 110 repeat families), and only ~1200 maternal genes repressed (13 repeat families) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: In Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos, only ~1200 maternal genes are repressed.
source: In contrast, Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos fail to properly activate the zygotic genome, with only 666 genes becoming activated (and 110 repeat families), and only ~1200 maternal genes repressed (13 repeat families) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: In Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos, 13 repeat families are repressed.
source: In contrast, Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos fail to properly activate the zygotic genome, with only 666 genes becoming activated (and 110 repeat families), and only ~1200 maternal genes repressed (13 repeat families) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—source data 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Hierarchical clustering shows that Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos are more similar to oocytes than to control 2C embryos.
source: Hierarchical clustering of Kdm1afl/fl oocytes, Kdm1aZp3 oocytes, Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos and Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos confirms this failure to activate the zygotic genome. Specifically, though Kdm1afl/fl oocytes are similar to Kdm1aZp3 oocytes, Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos are more similar to Kdm1afl/fl oocytes than Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Principal component analysis shows that ~40% of the variance between samples can be explained by a single component (PC1).
source: In addition, principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated that ~40% of the variance between Kdm1afl/fl oocytes, Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos, and Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos can be explained by a single component (PC1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and the heat maps generated from PC1 genes confirm that Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos have expression profiles more similar to Kdm1afl/fl oocytes than Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by PCA shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Heat maps from PC1 genes confirm that Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos have expression profiles more similar to oocytes than control 2C embryos.
source: In addition, principal component analysis (PCA) demonstrated that ~40% of the variance between Kdm1afl/fl oocytes, Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos, and Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos can be explained by a single component (PC1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), and the heat maps generated from PC1 genes confirm that Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos have expression profiles more similar to Kdm1afl/fl oocytes than Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by heat map analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: PC1 genes fall into two categories: those associated with unfertilized oocytes and those associated with early embryonic development.
source: GO analysis demonstrated that PC1 genes fall into two categories, those associated with unfertilized oocytes and are highly expressed in oocytes and Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos, and those associated with early embryonic development which are enriched only in Kdm1afl/fl M+Z+ 2C embryos (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis of PC1 genes.

claim: The major defect in the transcriptome of Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos is a failure to undergo the MZT.
source: Taken together, these data confirm that the major defect in the transcriptome of Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ 2C embryos is a failure to undergo the MZT.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined RNA-seq and analysis data.

claim: The majority of Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ embryos arrest prior to the blastocyst stage.
source: Similar to Kdm1aGdf9 and Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos, the majority of Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ embryos arrest prior to the blastocyst stage (Figure 4A–E).
evidence: This is supported by embryo staging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In control Kdm1aVasa M+Z+ embryos at e3.5, 55% have reached the blastocyst stage, 35% are multicellular, and 10% are fragmented/degraded.
source: In control Kdm1aVasa M+Z+ embryos at e3.5, 55% of embryos have reached the blastocyst stage, 35% are multicellular (>2C) and 10% are fragmented/degraded (n=37, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryo staging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: At e3.5, 85% of Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ embryos have fragmented/degraded.
source: In contrast, at e3.5 85% of the Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ embryos have fragmented/degraded (n=35, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryo staging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: By e3.5, 6% of Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ embryos have reached the multicellular stage and 5% are blastocysts.
source: However, unlike Kdm1aGdf9 and Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ embryos, which undergo complete embryonic arrest at the 1-2C stage, by e3.5 6% of Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ embryos have reached the multicellular stage (>2C) and 5% are blastocysts (n=35, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of embryo staging data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Some Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ embryos survive to birth.
source: Remarkably, some of these Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ embryos survive to birth.
evidence: This is based on observation of litter sizes.

claim: The average litter size born from Kdm1aVasa mutant mothers is 2.3.
source: The average litter size born from Kdm1aVasa mutant mothers is 2.3 (n=20), versus 6.2 (n=32) born from littermate control mothers (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of litter sizes shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The average litter size born from control mothers is 6.2.
source: The average litter size born from Kdm1aVasa mutant mothers is 2.3 (n=20), versus 6.2 (n=32) born from littermate control mothers (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of litter sizes shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The vast majority of time vaginal plugged Kdm1aVasa mutant mothers give rise to no viable progeny.
source: However, the vast majority of time vaginal plugged Kdm1aVasa mutant mothers give rise to no viable progeny.
evidence: This is based on observation of breeding outcomes.

claim: 5% of offspring born from littermate Kdm1aVasa control mothers die perinatally during the first 48 hr after birth.
source: Consistent with this being a major developmental transition, even in genotypically normal mice, we observe that 5% of offspring (n=216) born from littermate Kdm1aVasa control mothers die perinatally during the first 48 hr after birth (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of perinatal lethality shown in Figure 4G.

claim: 26% of Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ progeny die perinatally during the first 48 hr after birth.
source: However, in Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ progeny, the percentage of perinatal lethality is significantly increased (26%, n=47) (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of perinatal lethality shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The increase in perinatal lethality in Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ progeny is consistent with these animals having more subtle developmental defects.
source: However, this increase in perinatal lethality is consistent with these animals having more subtle developmental defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed perinatal lethality.

claim: Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults exhibit abnormal behaviors including excessive scratching and digging, along with food harassing.
source: These abnormal behaviors include excessive scratching and digging, along with food harassing, where animals grind up all of the remaining food in the food hopper and incorporate it into the bedding (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral observations and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: Over a 3-day period, each individual Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adult almost completely depleted the food in the food hopper due to food grinding and harassing.
source: Over a 3-day period, each individual Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adult almost completely depleted the food in the food hopper due to food grinding and harassing (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of food weight shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Food grinding in Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults results in a large increase in the height of the bedding over a 6-day period.
source: This resulted in a correspondingly large increase in the height of the bedding over a 6-day period (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of bedding height shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Food grinding behavior is not observed in Kdm1aVasa mutant mothers or the M. castaneus animals to which they were mated.
source: These effects are not observed in Kdm1aVasa mutant mothers or the M. castaneus animals to which they were mated (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,E), indicating that the behavior may be due to a maternal effect.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in figures.

claim: Intercrossing affected Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults produces no F2 intercrossed M+Z+ adults with the food-grinding behavior.
source: Intercrossing affected M-Z+ F1 hybrids produced no F2 intercrossed M+Z+ adults with the food-grinding behavior, suggesting that the food-grinding behavior is dependent upon a maternal effect (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from intercross experiments.

claim: The food-grinding behavior is dependent upon a maternal effect.
source: Intercrossing affected M-Z+ F1 hybrids produced no F2 intercrossed M+Z+ adults with the food-grinding behavior, suggesting that the food-grinding behavior is dependent upon a maternal effect (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,G).
evidence: This is inferred from the intercross experiments.

claim: Control B6/CAST hybrids exhibit modest food-grinding behavior.
source: These control hybrids exhibit modest food-grinding behavior, suggesting that the hybrid strain background likely also contributes to the maternal food-grinding defect (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data from control hybrids.

claim: The hybrid strain background likely contributes to the maternal food-grinding defect.
source: These control hybrids exhibit modest food-grinding behavior, suggesting that the hybrid strain background likely also contributes to the maternal food-grinding defect (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,F).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of food-grinding in control hybrids.

claim: The abnormal behavior is not due to Kdm1a haploinsufficiency.
source: Importantly, we also do not observe any Kdm1a haploinsufficiency defects. For example, the F2 intercrossed M+Z+ adults that are heterozygous for Kdm1a do not exhibit this abnormal behavior (Figure 5D,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,G). This suggests that the abnormal behavior is not due to Kdm1a haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that heterozygous F2 animals do not show the behavior.

claim: Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults bury 90% of marbles in 25 min in the marble-burying assay.
source: Compared to M. castaneus controls, which bury 25% in 25 min (Figure 5G,I, Video 2), Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults bury 90% in the same time period (Figure 5H,I, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of marble burying shown in Figure 5I.

claim: M. castaneus controls bury 25% of marbles in 25 min in the marble-burying assay.
source: Compared to M. castaneus controls, which bury 25% in 25 min (Figure 5G,I, Video 2), Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults bury 90% in the same time period (Figure 5H,I, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of marble burying shown in Figure 5I.

claim: F2 intercrossed M+Z+ adults do not exhibit excessive marble-burying behavior.
source: Similar to what was observed in the food-grinding assays, we do not observe this behavior in F2 intercrossed M+Z+ adults (average 7 marbles, Figure 5I), but we do see slightly elevated marble-burying in B6/CAST hybrid controls (average 10, Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of marble burying shown in Figure 5I.

claim: B6/CAST hybrid controls show slightly elevated marble-burying behavior.
source: Similar to what was observed in the food-grinding assays, we do not observe this behavior in F2 intercrossed M+Z+ adults (average 7 marbles, Figure 5I), but we do see slightly elevated marble-burying in B6/CAST hybrid controls (average 10, Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of marble burying shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults are significantly more affected than B6/CAST hybrid M+Z+ controls in marble-burying behavior.
source: Nevertheless, as in the food-grinding assay, Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults are significantly more affected than B6/CAST hybrid M+Z+ controls (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of quantification data.

claim: The excessive digging behavior is predominantly due to a maternal effect.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the excessive digging behavior is also predominantly due to a maternal effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined behavioral data.

claim: Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults perform significantly fewer movements across the middle of the cage in the open-field test.
source: Consistent with the behavioral defects that we observe in food-grinding and marble-burying, Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults perform significantly fewer movements across the middle of the cage (Figure 5J) and spend less time in the center overall than CAST controls (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of open field test data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults spend less time in the center of the cage in the open-field test than CAST controls.
source: Consistent with the behavioral defects that we observe in food-grinding and marble-burying, Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ adults perform significantly fewer movements across the middle of the cage (Figure 5J) and spend less time in the center overall than CAST controls (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of open field test data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Four genes that are known to maternally affect DNA methylation at imprinted loci (Tet1, Trim28, Zfp57 and Dppa3/Stella) are all misregulated in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ mutants.
source: For example, four genes that are known to maternally affect DNA methylation at imprinted loci, Tet1, Trim28, Zfp57 and Dppa3/Stella (Dawlaty et al., 2013; Li et al., 2008; Messerschmidt et al., 2012; Nakamura et al., 2007; Yamaguchi et al., 2013), are all misregulated in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+mutants (Tet1: -3.8 fold, Trim28: -3.3 fold, Zfp57: +3.2 fold and Dppa3/Stella: +.58 fold, Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Figure 3—source data 1B, quantitative RT-PCR validation of Trim28, Zfp57 and Dppa3/Stella in Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in figures.

claim: The DNA methyltransferase DNMT1 is overexpressed in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ mutants.
source: Additionally, the DNA methyltransferase DNMT1 is overexpressed in Kdm1aZp3 M-Z+ mutants (Dnmt1: +2.1 fold, Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Figure 3—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in figures.

claim: DNMT1 is thought to primarily act as the maintenance DNA methyltransferase.
source: DNMT1 is thought to primarily act as the maintenance DNA methyltransferase (Li et al., 1992; Pradhan et al., 1999), but when overexpressed, DNMT1 has been shown to have de novo DNA methyltransferase activity (Vertino et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When overexpressed, DNMT1 has been shown to have de novo DNA methyltransferase activity.
source: DNMT1 is thought to primarily act as the maintenance DNA methyltransferase (Li et al., 1992; Pradhan et al., 1999), but when overexpressed, DNMT1 has been shown to have de novo DNA methyltransferase activity (Vertino et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: DNA methylation and monoallelic expression at imprinted genes could be altered in Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ progeny.
source: Taken together, these observations raise the possibility that DNA methylation and monoallelic expression at imprinted genes could be altered in Kdm1aVasa M-Z+ progeny, either directly or indirectly.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed misregulation of epigenetic regulators.

claim: At Zac1, DNA methylation is inappropriately acquired on the paternal allele in both MEP.
source: At Zac1, DNA methylation is inappropriately acquired on the paternal allele in both MEP, though to a slightly lesser extent in MEP2 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Inappropriate paternal methylation at Zac1 is associated with significantly less expression of Zac1 in both MEP.
source: This is associated with significantly less expression of Zac1 in both MEP (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Zac1 is normally expressed exclusively from the paternal allele.
source: Moreover, Zac1 is normally expressed exclusively from the paternal allele (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific expression data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In MEP1, Zac1 is expressed exclusively from the maternal allele.
source: However, in MEP1 Zac1 is now expressed exclusively from the maternal allele, while in MEP2, the slightly lower level of inappropriate paternal methylation is associated with biallelic expression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific expression data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In MEP2, Zac1 shows biallelic expression.
source: However, in MEP1 Zac1 is now expressed exclusively from the maternal allele, while in MEP2, the slightly lower level of inappropriate paternal methylation is associated with biallelic expression (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific expression data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: At Impact, the overall DNA methylation pattern is unchanged.
source: At Impact, the overall DNA methylation pattern is unchanged (Figure 6D), but there is a dramatic change in expression.
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Impact is normally expressed exclusively from the paternal allele.
source: Impact is normally expressed exclusively from the paternal allele, but in both MEP1 and 2, Impact is now expressed predominantly from the maternal allele (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific expression data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In both MEP1 and MEP2, Impact is expressed predominantly from the maternal allele.
source: Impact is normally expressed exclusively from the paternal allele, but in both MEP1 and 2, Impact is now expressed predominantly from the maternal allele (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by allele-specific expression data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In both MEP1 and MEP2, there is a significant decrease in the overall expression level of Impact.
source: In addition, in both MEP1 and MEP2, there is a significant decrease in the overall expression level of Impact (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: At H19, DNA methylation is inappropriately lost on the paternal allele in MEP1.
source: For example, at H19 DNA methylation is inappropriately lost on the paternal allele in MEP1 (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: At H19, there is a slight acquisition of inappropriate methylation on the maternal allele of both MEP.
source: There is also a slight acquisition of inappropriate methylation on the maternal allele of both MEP (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: At Igf2r, DNA methylation is altered.
source: At two of these additional imprinted loci (H19 and Igf2r), DNA methylation is altered (Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in figures.

claim: At Mest and Snrpn, DNA methylation appears normal.
source: At two additional imprinted genes (Mest and Snrpn), DNA methylation appears normal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,E).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data shown in figures.

claim: At Igf2r, Mest, and Snrpn, there is an overall decrease in gene expression.
source: Furthermore, at three of the additional imprinted loci, we observe an overall decrease in gene expression. These include Igf2r, Mest, and Snrpn (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D,F), while at H19, expression levels are unaffected (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in figures.

claim: At H19, expression levels are unaffected.
source: Furthermore, at three of the additional imprinted loci, we observe an overall decrease in gene expression. These include Igf2r, Mest, and Snrpn (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,D,F), while at H19, expression levels are unaffected (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: The allele-specific expression of Igf2r, Mest, Snrpn, and H19 remains unaffected.
source: However, the allele-specific expression of all of these additional imprinted loci remains unaffected (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on allele-specific expression analysis.

claim: The changes in DNA methylation and expression indicate a general disruption in the normal regulation of genomic imprinting.
source: Taken together, the changes in DNA methylation and expression indicate a general disruption in the normal regulation of genomic imprinting.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined imprinting data.

claim: The maternal reprogramming function of KDM1A is conserved between C. elegans and mammals.
source: As in C. elegans, KDM1A is heavily deposited maternally in the mouse oocyte, suggesting that KDM1A could play a conserved role in maternal reprogramming (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the expression data and phenotypic similarities.

claim: Maternal KDM1A is essential for the progression of mammalian embryogenesis.
source: Thus, maternal KDM1A is essential for the progression of mammalian embryogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the embryonic arrest phenotype.

claim: The observed 1-2C embryonic arrest does not rule out an additional role for KDM1A in oocyte maturation.
source: The observed 1-2C embryonic arrest does not rule out an additional role for KDM1A in oocyte maturation, as we observe that a small fraction of KDM1A deficient oocytes are unfertilized, fertilized with multiple sperm, or display other gross morphological defects, including loss of the zona pellucida.
evidence: This is based on observation of occasional oocyte defects.

claim: Kim et al. have reported that deletion of a different conditional Kdm1a allele with Zp3-Cre results in defects in meiotic progression.
source: Consistent with this, Kim et al. have recently reported that deletion of a different conditional Kdm1a allele with Zp3-Cre results in defects in meiotic progression (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to another study.

claim: In Kdm1aGdf9 and Kdm1aZp3 mutants, the majority of oocytes are fertilized normally.
source: Nevertheless, in Kdm1aGdf9 and Kdm1aZp3 mutants, we find that the majority of oocytes are fertilized normally, and many embryos undergo cleavage to reach the 2C stage (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on observation of embryo development.

claim: In hypomorphic Kdm1aVasa animals, defects are observed on the paternal allele of imprinted loci.
source: Also, in hypomorphic Kdm1aVasa animals we observe defects on the paternal allele of imprinted loci (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by bisulfite sequencing data.

claim: The results suggest a requirement for KDM1A post-fertilization in the zygote.
source: These results suggest a requirement for KDM1A post-fertilization in the zygote.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations.

claim: In mammals, zygotic transcription initiates between the one and two cell stage.
source: In mammals, zygotic transcription initiates between the one and two cell stage (Aoki et al., 1997; Hamatani et al., 2004; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Heterozygous offspring derived from maternal deletion crosses likely begin to express KDM1A from paternal allele at the 2C stage.
source: As a result, the heterozygous offspring derived from our crosses likely begin to express KDM1A from paternal allele at the 2C stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of zygotic gene activation.

claim: The results pinpoint a requirement for maternal KDM1A reprogramming between fertilization and cleavage.
source: Taken together, these results pinpoint a requirement for maternal KDM1A reprogramming between fertilization and cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data.

claim: Chemically inhibiting KDM1A function post-fertilization results in a 2C arrest.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, the accompanying paper by Ancelin et al. demonstrates that chemically inhibiting KDM1A function post-fertilization also results in a 2C arrest.
evidence: This is supported by reference to the accompanying paper.

claim: The difference in phenotype between Gdf9-Cre and Zp3-Cre deletions suggests that KDM1A may act maternally at multiple discrete steps.
source: Nevertheless, the difference in phenotype suggests that KDM1A may act maternally at multiple discrete steps.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic differences between Cre lines.

claim: The observation that many maternally deleted embryos undergo cleavage suggests that KDM1A is not just required for cell-cycle progression or cell viability.
source: Importantly, the observation that many maternally deleted embryos undergo cleavage, suggests that KDM1A is not just required for cell-cycle progression or cell viability (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that embryos can cleave.

claim: KDM1A null embryos survive until e8.
source: This conclusion is consistent with the observation that KDM1A null embryos survive until e8 (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The difference in phenotype between maternally deleted embryos and embryonically deleted embryos clearly delineates the maternal requirement for KDM1A from the embryonic requirement.
source: Furthermore, the difference in phenotype between maternally deleted embryos and embryonically deleted embryos, which survive to e8, clearly delineates the maternal requirement for KDM1A from the embryonic requirement.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes.

claim: Maternally deleted Kdm1a embryos fail to undergo the MZT.
source: This indicates that maternally deleted Kdm1a embryos fail to undergo the MZT.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data.

claim: The requirement for KDM1A in facilitating the MZT is demonstrated in the accompanying paper by Ancelin et al.
source: The requirement for KDM1A in facilitating the MZT is also demonstrated in the accompanying paper by Ancelin et al., where it is shown that maternal KDM1A is necessary for the multiple waves of zygotic gene activation.
evidence: This is supported by reference to the accompanying paper.

claim: KDM1A plays a major role in facilitating the progression of embryogenesis by enabling the MZT.
source: Thus, we propose that KDM1A plays a major role in facilitating the progression of embryogenesis by enabling the MZT.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data.

claim: Tet1/Tet2 double mutants exhibit a partial perinatal lethality phenotype reminiscent of what is observed in Kdm1aVasa progeny.
source: For example, Tet1/Tet2 double mutants exhibit a partial perinatal lethality phenotype that is reminiscent of what we observe in Kdm1aVasa progeny (Dawlaty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Mice that are haploinsufficient for Trim28 display abnormal exploratory behaviors.
source: Also, mice that are haploinsufficient for Trim28 display abnormal exploratory behaviors (Whitelaw et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The removal of H3K4 methylation may be required to enable the activity of the DNMT3a/3b de novo methyltransferase complex.
source: For example, the removal of H3K4 methylation may be required to enable the activity of the DNMT3a/3b de novo methyltransferase complex (Ooi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A model has been proposed to account for the imprinting defects observed when KDM1B is maternally deleted.
source: Such a model has been proposed to account for the imprinting defects that are observed when KDM1B is maternally deleted (Ciccone et al., 2009; Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The accompanying paper by Ancelin et al. demonstrates that loss of KDM1A maternally leads to global changes in both H3K4 and H3K9 methylation following fertilization.
source: Consistent with this model, the accompanying paper by Ancelin et al. demonstrates that loss of KDM1A maternally leads to global changes in both H3K4 and H3K9 methylation following fertilization.
evidence: This is supported by reference to the accompanying paper.

claim: Stewart et al. demonstrated that loss of maternal KDM1A in mice does not affect H3K4me2 or the acquisition of DNA methylation at imprinted genes.
source: However, Stewart et al. recently demonstrated that loss of maternal KDM1A in mice does not affect H3K4me2, or the acquisition of DNA methylation at imprinted genes (Stewart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The variable disruption of imprinting in hypomorphic animals is more consistent with a general disruption of epigenetic information.
source: Moreover, the variable disruption of imprinting that we observe in hypomorphic animals is more consistent with a general disruption of epigenetic information.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed imprinting defects.

claim: The general disruption of epigenetic reprogramming, along with secondary epigenetic defects due to misregulation of epigenetic reprogramming enzymes during the MZT, combine to give rise to the phenomena that manifest postnatally in progeny.
source: Thus, we favor a model in which the general disruption of epigenetic reprogramming, along with secondary epigenetic defects due to the misregulation of epigenetic reprogramming enzymes during the MZT, combine to give rise to the phenomena that manifest postnatally in progeny.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined data.

claim: Both Zac1 and Impact have been associated with nervous system defects.
source: Interestingly, both Zac1 and Impact have been associated with nervous system defects, and loss of Zac1 paternally results in perinatal lethality (Chung et al., 2011; Kosaki et al., 2001; Pereira et al., 2005; Roffe et al., 2013; Schmidt-Edelkraut et al., 2014; Varrault et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of Zac1 paternally results in perinatal lethality.
source: Interestingly, both Zac1 and Impact have been associated with nervous system defects, and loss of Zac1 paternally results in perinatal lethality (Chung et al., 2011; Kosaki et al., 2001; Pereira et al., 2005; Roffe et al., 2013; Schmidt-Edelkraut et al., 2014; Varrault et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The results establish a novel mammalian paradigm in which altered epigenetic reprogramming by a histone demethylase between generations leads to defects that manifest weeks later.
source: Nevertheless, our results establish a novel mammalian paradigm in which altered epigenetic reprogramming by a histone demethylase between generations leads to defects that manifest weeks later, highlighting the potential long-range consequences of epigenetic perturbations in the early mammalian embryo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined findings of the study.

claim: The results highlight the potential long-range consequences of epigenetic perturbations in the early mammalian embryo.
source: Nevertheless, our results establish a novel mammalian paradigm in which altered epigenetic reprogramming by a histone demethylase between generations leads to defects that manifest weeks later, highlighting the potential long-range consequences of epigenetic perturbations in the early mammalian embryo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined findings of the study.
